model.one_line: A foundation model for experiment design in biotech, biochemical and chemical development: it reads a campaign's results so far and proposes which experiments to run next.

Proposals for the next experiment or the next batch

Ranking a candidate list (for example a plate of untested formulations) by expected outcome
Campaigns that aim for a target value, stay within limits, or trade off several outcomes

capabilities.name: Batches
capabilities.text: Proposes a whole batch at once, from a single experiment to a full plate.

capabilities.name: Targets, not just maxima
capabilities.text: Aim for a value (for example 50% yield within a tolerance) and get the probability of landing in range.

capabilities.name: Failed runs and saturated readouts
capabilities.text: Declare where runs fail or a readout saturates; the model reads those results as limits, not exact values.

capabilities.name: Limits on other outcomes
capabilities.text: Keep cost, purity or other measured outcomes within limits while optimising one.

capabilities.name: Several objectives
capabilities.text: See the trade-off between competing outcomes and choose where to sit on it.

capabilities.name: Mixed parameter types
capabilities.text: Continuous, integer, log-scale, categorical parameters and mixtures that must sum to a total.

capabilities.name: No per-campaign tuning
capabilities.text: Nothing is fitted or tuned per campaign: the model reads the history and predicts directly.

enables.title: Every plate ranked
enables.text: A team screening one plate a week gets the next plate proposed and every candidate ranked, so reagent goes to the wells most likely to win or to teach the most.

enables.title: Failed runs count as information
enables.text: Campaigns where many conditions fail (precipitation, no growth, no signal) or a readout saturates can declare those limits instead of hiding or deleting the runs.

enables.title: Aim for a value, not just the maximum
enables.text: Hitting 50% yield within a tolerance, or a viscosity window, is a goal in its own right, with the probability of landing in range for every proposal.

enables.title: No modelling expertise per campaign
enables.text: There is no model to fit, kernel to choose or setting to tune: the lab supplies its results so far and gets the next experiments.

enables.title: From a few parameters to many
enables.text: The same model serves a two-factor optimisation and a formulation with dozens of components, mixing continuous, categorical and mixture parameters.

category_explainer.title: What is a foundation model for experiment design?
category_explainer.text: Classical design of experiments plans a screen up front. Bayesian optimisation fits a new statistical model to every campaign and starts from scratch each time. A foundation model for experiment design arrives ready: it already knows how lab results tend to depend on settings, from smooth trends to sharp optima, thresholds and failed runs. Given a lab's results so far, it predicts how untested settings will turn out and proposes the next experiments in seconds.

asides.title: How it works
asides.text: Given a campaign's results so far, [MODEL NAME] predicts untested settings in a single pass: a full distribution over the outcome and the chance the run succeeds, with no model to fit or tune. It then proposes the settings with the most to gain.

asides.title: How these benchmarks were run
asides.text: Every method started from the same initial experiments on the same seeds and ran through the same test setup. Industry tools ran with their default settings. Every benchmark was held out of training.

faq.q: Does it need my historical data?
faq.a: No. It is ready for a new campaign from the first results. Earlier results from the same campaign make its next proposals better.

faq.q: How many parameters can a campaign have?
faq.a: Up to 100 per campaign: continuous, integer, log-scale and categorical parameters, and mixtures that must add up to a total.

faq.q: Can it handle failed runs and saturated readouts?
faq.a: Yes. Declare where runs fail or a readout saturates and the model reads those results as limits, not exact values.

faq.q: Can it aim for a value instead of the maximum?
faq.a: Yes. Set a target with a tolerance and it proposes the settings most likely to land in range, with that probability for each.

faq.q: How does it compare with design of experiments?
faq.a: We benchmarked it against both a space-filling screen and a classical response-surface design; the results are above.
